title: Advanced chemical analysis
text: Turning the Global Framework on Chemicals into measurable progress requires reliable evidence of chemical pollution. UKCEH’s laboratories provide that evidence, from measuring trace levels of chemicals in water, soil and wildlife to imaging individual particles at the nanoscale.

title: Advanced chemical analysis
text:
Analytical Chemistry laboratories
UKCEH’s analytical chemistry laboratories in Lancaster measure a wide range of pollutants in soil, sediment, water and biological samples. Our data underpin environmental monitoring and chemical risk assessment, helping policymakers, regulators and partners understand where contamination occurs and whether the remediation measures put in place are proving effective.

Chemicals we measure

PFAS (“forever chemicals”). Quantitative analysis of approximately 50 compounds, including carboxylic acids, sulfonic acids, sulfonamides, fluorotelomers and emerging PFAS.
Chemicals in plastics. Plasticisers and tyre additives such as 6PPD, measured alongside plastic particles to give a fuller picture of plastic-related pollution.
Organic contaminants. Persistent organic pollutants, pesticides, pharmaceuticals and emerging environmental contaminants.
Metals and metalloids. Trace measurements in environmental samples to support pollution monitoring and assessment.
Stable isotopes. Isotopic analysis to support studies of environmental processes and sources.



Finding what we weren’t looking for
Alongside targeted analysis of known chemicals, we use non-target screening (a broad scan for unexpected or unidentified substances) to detect chemicals of growing concern, including novel and emerging PFAS, pharmaceuticals, pesticides and other chemicals.


Quality you can rely on
Our laboratories are UKAS-accredited to ISO/IEC 17025:2017 and operate rigorous quality assurance, sample tracking and contamination control, so you can have confidence in the measurements that inform monitoring and decisions.


Supporting international and national programmes
We contribute to many international and national programmes, helping to track progress, identify emerging risks and inform action on chemical pollution. These include:

PARC, the European Partnership for the Assessment of Risks from Chemicals
Short-chain PFAS inter-laboratory studies
The National Honey Monitoring Scheme, through Defra’s BEECH project
The Predatory Bird Monitoring Scheme
The Chemicals Investigations Programme (CIP)



Work with us
To discuss analysis for your project or monitoring programme, contact enquiries@ceh.ac.uk.

title: Advanced chemical analysis
text:
CoreMiS



The RISE-EDS microscope (left) and a Zeiss light microscope (right) at CoreMiS.


The Centre for Multimodal Correlative Microscopy and Spectroscopy (CoreMiS) is the first platform in the UK dedicated to micro-spectroscopic analysis of environmental samples by Raman Imaging and Spectroscopy with Scanning Electron Microscopy and Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (RISE-EDS).
RISE-EDS allows us to see in tiny detail chemical reactions in water, atmosphere, soil and plants.
Despite the recognition of the common importance of nanoscale phenomena for governing the behaviour of pollutants, scientists to date have relied on measurements made in bulk or, at best, at the microscale to infer these critical nanoscale processes. Without nanoscale understanding, it will remain challenging to identify, understand and manage exposure to environmental pollutants and the resulting health and ecological impacts.

title: Advanced chemical analysis
text:
The Microplastics Analysis Facility
The purpose of the Microplastics Analysis Facility is to detect the presence of plastics in the environment so that researchers can understand their fate, bioavailability and interactions with wildlife. This research helps governments, consumers and industry to tackle the growing pollution and harm caused by plastic litter and microplastic particles in the environment – in our soils, freshwaters, oceans and food chains.



Microplastics in moss under the microscope.


The facility has undertaken work across public and private sectors investigating the prevalence of microplastics in our natural world. For example, we identified the widespread deposition of microplastics from the air across rural areas of the United Kingdom, as part of the Working Group on Effects (WGE) of the Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution (LRTAP). Baseline assessments such as this, and our work investigating microplastics in the UK water industry, are essential in tracking progress against societal, government and industry priorities, to reduce the emissions and potential harm of plastics and microplastics in the environment.

title: Global Framework on Chemicals
text:
The UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology is an independent, not-for-profit, environmental science organisation that ensures society understands how the environment is changing and what that means for people and nature. Through our science, data, and partnerships, we work across the UK and globally to turn evidence into better decisions, actions and a more resilient future.

We are taking part in the first International Conference of the Global Framework on Chemicals (IC1). Join us at the Action and Partnerships Hub to discover how our scientists bring long-term environmental monitoring, chemical risk assessment and pollution modelling to the conversation, helping to turn the Framework’s targets into measurable progress and actionable insights on the ground.
Healthy environments underpin healthy economies, resilient communities and sustainable growth. Yet understanding whether actions to address pollution are working requires robust evidence that connects data and understanding across air, water, soil and wildlife. The UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology (UKCEH) works with governments, international organisations and partners to generate, integrate and interpret environmental evidence that supports decision-making on chemicals and pollution.

title: Monitoring chemicals in the environment
text: Knowing whether the Global Framework on Chemicals is working means measuring chemicals in the environment consistently, over decades. UKCEH runs some of the longest-running chemical monitoring schemes in the world. They detect emerging threats to wildlife and show whether restrictions on harmful chemicals are delivering the intended benefits.

title: Monitoring chemicals in the environment
text:
Predatory Bird Monitoring Scheme
The Predatory Bird Monitoring Scheme (PBMS) tracks contaminants in the livers and eggs of predatory birds across Britain. Birds of prey sit at the top of food chains, where persistent chemicals accumulate, which makes them sensitive sentinels for the wider environment.
The scheme was set up in 1962 by the Nature Conservancy at Monks Wood to study the effects of organochlorine insecticides and organomercury fungicides on birds and mammals. That research contributed to these chemicals being banned from farming in Britain and elsewhere, and declining residues in birds and eggs then showed that the bans were working. PBMS is the longest-running scheme of its kind anywhere in the world.
Since then, the scheme has expanded as new concerns have emerged. It now monitors:

Anticoagulant rodenticides in barn owls (since 1983), kestrels and red kites
Lead, mercury and 15 other elements in red kites, sparrowhawks and gannet eggs
Brominated flame retardants (PBDEs) in common buzzard, otters and sparrowhawk eggs
PFAS (“forever chemicals”) in common buzzards

Members of the public normally send in birds of prey they find dead, and the scheme receives up to 400 carcasses and 200 eggs each year. Public submissions are currently paused because of avian influenza, so the team is working with wildlife professionals and trained citizen scientists to collect birds instead. Samples dating back to the late 1960s are kept in a tissue archive of more than 100,000 samples, which means chemicals that were not recognised as a concern at the time can still be measured in historical samples.
PBMS data feed directly into policy. The scheme reports annually on rodenticides in barn owls for the UK Rodenticide Stewardship regime. Its team also led the design of the interim indicator on managing exposure to chemicals for the UK Government’s 25 Year Environment Plan, for which it is the principal source of monitoring data. PBMS is funded by the Natural Environment Research Council (through UKCEH’s National Capability programme), Natural England and the Campaign for Responsible Rodenticide Use.

title: Monitoring chemicals in the environment
text:
National Honey Monitoring Scheme
The National Honey Monitoring Scheme (NHMS) works with beekeepers to use honeybees as monitors of the UK countryside. Honeybees forage over large areas around their hives, so each jar of honey captures what is happening across the surrounding landscape. Monitoring for pesticides is funded by Defra under the project BEECH (Biomonitoring Environmental Exposures of Chemicals using Honeybees). It is the only national, multi-year biomonitoring system for pollinators’ exposure to pesticides in the UK.
Since 2018, beekeepers across the UK have sent in honey samples, growing from 202 samples in the first year to nearly 1,500 by 2022. The scheme now sends out up to 1,000 sampling packs each year. Each sample can be analysed in several ways:

Pollen DNA barcoding identifies which plants the bees have been foraging on, by region and season
Pesticide screening measures residues of 135 pesticides. This has run every year since 2019
Hive records from beekeepers, including honey yield, colony losses and disease, link exposure to colony health
Satellite mapping of crops and habitats around each apiary connects results to land use

The latest results show that pollinators’ real-world exposure to pesticides is declining, with marked reductions in both the number of active ingredients detected and the overall risk to honeybees since a peak in 2021. Approved pyrethroid insecticides still account for most of the risk, although they are detected less often. Most withdrawn and older insecticides are fading from honey, and the neonicotinoid clothianidin is the only one of these still detected frequently.
The monitoring also shows that:

Long-term, low-level exposure (chronic exposure) to pesticides typical of agricultural conditions puts honeybees at risk, and synergistic interactions between some fungicides and insecticides may increase that risk considerably
Land use around the hive is a key predictor: hives surrounded by more arable and horticultural land have more residues, at higher levels, and face higher acute and chronic risk
Exposure varies substantially from year to year, which is why sustained monitoring matters

This gives an evidence base that is not available from pesticide usage surveys, modelling or regulatory risk assessments alone.
The same approach can detect other emerging contaminants. Honey samples have revealed human pharmaceuticals that may reach the landscape through sewage sludge spread on land, and the scheme will soon be used to look for PFAS.

title: Prioritising actions
text: Regulators, policymakers and governments need evidence about which chemicals cause the most harm, where and to what, and whether the measures they take are working. For more than sixty years, UKCEH science has provided that evidence and has led directly to regulatory action to reduce chemical pollution.

title: Prioritising actions
text:
From evidence to action

Organochlorine insecticides

1960s
Evidence. In the 1960s, research at Monks Wood linked organochlorine insecticides such as DDT and dieldrin, and organomercury fungicides, to declines in birds of prey. The Predatory Bird Monitoring Scheme, established in 1962, measured these chemicals in birds and their eggs.
Action. This evidence contributed to these chemicals being banned from farming in Britain and elsewhere. Monitoring then showed residues falling in birds and eggs, confirming that the bans were working.


Neonicotinoid insecticides

2016–2018
Evidence. A UKCEH-led analysis of 18 years of national records for 62 wild bee species linked neonicotinoid use on oilseed rape to long-term population declines. Species that forage on oilseed rape were affected three times more than other species. In 2017, a UKCEH-led field experiment across the UK, Germany and Hungary found that neonicotinoid-treated crops harmed honeybees and wild bees, although effects varied between countries.
Action. In late 2017, the UK’s Expert Committee on Pesticides advised ministers that the UKCEH field study “significantly adds to the evidence base”, and that the risk to pollinators was greater than previously thought. In April 2018, EU member states, including the UK, voted to ban all outdoor uses of the neonicotinoids clothianidin, imidacloprid and thiamethoxam. The National Honey Monitoring Scheme continues to track neonicotinoid residues in the environment after the ban.


Anticoagulant rodenticides

2016 onwards
Evidence. The Predatory Bird Monitoring Scheme has measured second-generation anticoagulant rodenticides in barn owls since 1983, showing how widely these rat poisons pass through food chains to non-target wildlife.
Action. Since 2016, the scheme has reported annually on rodenticides in barn owls for the UK Rodenticide Stewardship regime, which aims to reduce risks to wildlife. Its data were used in the regime’s five-year review.


Lead ammunition

2021–2029
Evidence. The Predatory Bird Monitoring Scheme analysed lead in 220 common buzzards found dead between 2007 and 2018. Lead isotope analysis showed that 57% of the lead in their livers came from shotgun pellets, rising to 89% in birds with the highest exposure. This study and PBMS data on sparrowhawks were cited in the Health and Safety Executive’s assessment of the risks of lead ammunition under UK REACH.
Action. In July 2025, the UK Government announced a ban on lead ammunition. The sale and use of lead shot and large-calibre lead bullets for live quarry shooting will end on 1 April 2029.


Acid rain and air pollution

1990s onwards
Evidence. UKCEH hosts the UK National Focal Centre for critical loads, which calculates and maps the levels of acid and nitrogen deposition that UK habitats can tolerate without harm. These maps underpin UK policy on acidification and eutrophication, and the UK’s contribution to international agreements such as the Gothenburg Protocol, which set national emission ceilings for sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and ammonia.
Action. As emissions have fallen, the area of acid-sensitive UK habitats receiving more acid deposition than they can tolerate fell by 28.5% between 1995 and 2014. Long-term monitoring of upland lakes and streams shows that their water chemistry is recovering.

title: Prioritising actions
text:
Assessing policy options
Before acting, decision-makers need to know which measures will reduce pollution the most, in which parts of the environment, and at what cost. UKCEH links models of chemical emissions, environmental fate and exposure, so that policy options can be compared before they are put in place.

Example: intentionally added microplastics
Defra option appraisal · 2025
Microplastics are intentionally added to many products, from detergents and cosmetics to the rubber infill used on synthetic sports pitches. Unlike microplastics from tyre wear or textiles, these can be controlled at source. For a Defra option appraisal supporting UK REACH, UKCEH and Economics for the Environment Consultancy (eftec) estimated UK emissions, exposure, risk and impacts of intentionally added microplastics to 2043. They then compared six options for reducing them, with the results published in Integrated Environmental Assessment and Management.


160,000 t
Intentionally added microplastics used in the UK, 2024–2043


50,000 t
Emitted to the environment over the same period


6
Policy options compared, from broad restrictions to targeted measures


£9/kg
Cost of the most cost-effective option: containing sports pitch infill


The UTOPIA model traced emissions from products to soils, rivers and seas. Synthetic sports surfaces were the largest single source. Because about 99% of microplastics reaching wastewater treatment are retained in sewage sludge, and most sludge is spread on farmland, agricultural soils receive the most overall.
The six options fell into three groups:

Restrictions on use (broad, targeted or aligned with the EU’s REACH restriction) gave the largest reductions in exposure across the environment, but at an average cost of £261–601 million per year. RMO 1A–1C.
Containment measures on synthetic sports pitches reduced exposure from sports surfaces as much as the restrictions did, for about £6 million per year. This was the most cost-effective option. RMO 2.
Reducing the amount of sewage sludge spread on land, by 95% or 50%, mainly benefited agricultural soils, at £10–60 million per year. It would also reduce soil exposure to other contaminants in sludge, such as pharmaceuticals. RMO 3A–3B.




Percentage reduction in predicted environmental concentrations of intentionally added microplastics in 2043 under each risk management option (RMO), compared with business as usual. RMO 1A–1C restrict use, RMO 2 contains sports pitch infill, and RMO 3A–3B reduce sewage sludge spread on land. Figure from Uluseker et al. (2026), CC BY 4.0.


No single option was best on every measure, but combining them, for example by containing sports pitch infill alongside a targeted restriction, could achieve most of the benefit at much lower cost. Defra is considering the findings, which will guide future decisions under UK REACH.
